title: Carved maple salt spoon
subtitle: A tiny pinch-salt spoon for a salt pig or cellar
excerpt: A small salt spoon in seasoned maple: 10 cm overall, a shallow oval bowl, and a short handle that rests across a salt pig without falling in. Knife-only work from a sawn blank, raw-linseed finish. A good first project for the detail knife.
sourceNotes: Traditional British salt-spoon patterns from Cassell's Dictionary of Cookery (1883) and the Museum of English Rural Life kitchen-ware collection, open access.

glossaryTerms.definition: Air-dried or kiln-dried wood at a stable moisture content for indoor use (8 to 12 per cent). Does not shrink after working.
A short straight-bladed knife with a stout handle; the Swedish school-craft standard for whittling and spoon-carving.
A leather strap charged with abrasive compound, used to maintain a sharp edge between honings.

content.text: A salt spoon is the smallest piece in the carved-spoon family. At 10 cm overall, it sits next to the salt pig on the worktop and lifts a measured pinch without spilling. This project uses
seasoned wood

rather than green, because the piece is so small that a green-wood blank would dry and crack within hours of being carved thin. Maple is the best choice: close-grained, hard, food-safe, and pale enough to show the salt clearly against the bowl.
Before you start cutting.
Grip: four-finger grip on the work; thumb-push grip on the knife. Never make a cut whose blade-path can reach a body part.
Cut direction: push cuts (blade away from body) and thumb-pivot cuts are the default. Pull cuts only with the work braced against the chest and the blade-arc unable to reach anything vital.
Sharpening: a dull tool is more dangerous than a sharp one. The dull tool slips. Strop every fifteen minutes of carving, hone weekly, oilstone monthly.
First aid: keep a styptic pencil, gauze, and a clean dressing within reach. Apply firm pressure, elevate, and dress. A cut that shows fat or won't close with pressure goes to A&E, not a plaster.
Workspace: stable seat, good light, no children or pets within arm-and-blade reach.
Wood
Maple in the
seasoned

state, ideally from a board 20 mm thick. A 12 cm length sawn from the board is the starting piece. Maple is dense and hard; it takes a clean knife edge without tearing at the fine sections needed for a small spoon. Cherry is a good alternative and turns a warmer red-brown with age. Sycamore also works but is softer and may mark more in daily salt use.
Tools
Sloyd knife: all handle and exterior bowl work.
Hook knife, small radius: for hollowing the bowl.
Detail knife (optional): for fine finishing at the rim and the handle tip.
Leather strop: strop every ten minutes on the hook knife.
Raw linseed oil: food-safe finish with a two-week cure.
There is no axe work on this project. Maple in the seasoned state is too hard for rough axe shaping at this scale; the
sloyd knife
handles all bulk removal.
Method
Step 1: Mark the blank

Draw the spoon on the face of the blank. The bowl is 3.5 cm long, 2.5 cm wide, 8 mm deep at the centre. The handle is 6.5 cm long, 1 cm wide at the shoulder, 7 mm at the tip. The spoon is entirely flat in plan at this stage; the thickness from board face to back is 18 to 20 mm, which gives enough depth for the bowl and the dome beneath it.
Step 2: Cut the plan silhouette with the sloyd knife

Hold the blank with a four-finger grip, thumb on top. Use push cuts with the sloyd knife to remove the waste outside the drawn profile. Maple is hard; keep the edge sharp and use thumb-pivot cuts for the curved bowl outline rather than long sweeping strokes.
Step 3: Thin the handle

Reduce the handle from 20 mm thick to 6 mm at mid-length. Push cuts along the long axis of the handle, working from both faces toward the centre. The handle is too small to hold safely with the four-finger grip; instead hold it between thumb and forefinger of the non-knife hand and work with short strokes aimed away from both hands.
Step 4: Dome the bowl back

Turn the blank over. Use push cuts to dome the underside of the bowl to a depth of 6 mm at the centre. The dome is what allows the bowl walls to be thin. Without the dome, the piece would be a flat slice of wood with a hollow pressed into it, which is too fragile to use.
Step 5: Hollow the bowl

Use the small hook knife to hollow the bowl. The bowl is 8 mm deep and 3.5 cm across. On a piece this small, the hook knife is working at close range. Secure the blank against a chopping block or a vice and work with one hand on the hook knife, keeping the non-knife hand behind the blade arc at all times. Short strokes, each removing a thin curl.
Maple resists the hook knife more than sycamore.
Strop
every ten minutes. If the knife is not cutting, it is compressing and burnishing the surface; hone before you continue.
Step 6: Refine and finish the rim

The rim of the bowl should be 3 to 4 mm thick and smooth to the lip. Use the detail knife, if available, to pare the rim to a clean edge. If using only the sloyd knife, angle the blade and use the tip to pare along the rim in short scooping strokes.
Finishing

Because the blank is already seasoned, the spoon can be oiled the same day. Apply raw linseed oil to all surfaces. On a piece this small, the oil soaks in within twenty minutes. Apply a second coat, leave one hour, wipe the surplus. Cure for two weeks before placing in contact with food. The cure is the same regardless of the size of the piece.
Variations
Cherry: takes on a deep red-brown tone over months of use and looks striking next to a pale salt pig.
Cut a hanging hole in the tip and fit a leather cord so the spoon hangs from the salt pig rim.
Decorate the handle with a simple kolrosing line down the centre using a marking knife and rubbed coffee grounds.
Care
Rinse under running water and dry immediately. Salt is hygroscopic and draws moisture into any crack in the finish. Keep the bowl oiled.

attrs.symptom: The hook knife is bouncing off the maple surface
attrs.cause: The edge is not sharp enough for the hardness of the wood.
attrs.fix: Hone on the 1000-grit waterstone before attempting the bowl on maple. Maple needs a sharper edge than sycamore or birch.

attrs.cause: The handle was thinned too fast, leaving one thin section that broke across the grain.
attrs.fix: Thin the handle gradually from both faces in alternate passes. Never remove more than 2 mm per face per pass.

attrs.symptom: The bowl rim is not level
attrs.cause: The dome on the back of the bowl is not centred, causing one side of the rim to be higher than the other.
attrs.fix: Check the rim with a straight edge. Re-cut the dome so it sits under the centre of the bowl, not offset to one side.
